extractedText: Field notes Long read · 10 min “ Why Indonesia's National AI Will Be Built by Telkom, Not KORIKA Two years in, the consortium built to deliver Indonesia's national AI strategy has shipped summits and papers while the real capability accrues inside Telkom and GoTo. Why the imported quadruple-helix model fits Jakarta poorly, and why the next vehicle will be a Telkom-led public-private partnership. Intelligence Desk Editorial Team 20 Jun 2026 Indonesia's national-AI ambition has plenty of forums. The shippable capability is being built on the factory floor. Illustration generated for AI in Asia. Advertisement Advertisement Key takeaways KORIKA, the multi-stakeholder body created to deliver Indonesia's national AI strategy, has produced summits, position papers and one niche health platform, but very little shippable product two years on. The country's genuine national-AI traction is coming from companies, namely Telkom's sovereign platform with IBM and GoTo's in-house model, and it is happening alongside KORIKA rather than because of it. The quadruple-helix consensus model was imported from European innovation policy and fits poorly with Jakarta's commercial reality, where the private sector adopts AI far faster than the state. Even Indonesia's flagship national AI roadmap was driven by a ministry, Komdigi, coordinating 39 agencies, not by the consortium that was meant to orchestrate the effort. The next workable national-AI vehicle is likely to be a Telkom-led public-private partnership with a commercial mandate, not another multi-stakeholder forum. Indonesia has the largest digital economy in Southeast Asia, a population of more than 280 million, and a national artificial intelligence strategy that runs to the year 2045. What it does not yet have is a national-AI institution that ships. The body created to fill that gap, KORIKA, the Collaboration for Research and Industrial Innovation in Artificial Intelligence, has spent the past two years convening the right people and producing the right documents. The trouble is that the actual products Indonesians can use are being built somewhere else entirely. The pattern is now hard to miss. Telkom launched a sovereign AI platform with IBM in June 2025. GoTo posted its first ever quarterly profit in 2025 while training a more efficient in-house large language model. Meanwhile the consortium tasked with leading the national effort held another summit. This essay argues that the gap is not an accident of timing. It is structural, it follows directly from the model KORIKA was built on, and it points to a different kind of vehicle for whatever comes next. Source KORIKA was established in 2021 as a direct outcome of Indonesia's National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, the Stranas KA 2020 to 2045. Its founding idea is collaboration across what its leaders call the quadruple helix, namely government, industry, academia and community. On paper it is the orchestration layer for the whole national effort, the table at which the strategy is supposed to turn into reality. Look at what the table has produced and the picture is thinner than the ambition. In 2025 KORIKA ran its AI Innovation Summit in Jakarta, a worthy convening that doubled as the venue for a government keynote on national strategy. Earlier in the year it helped launch a platform for forecasting climate-sensitive diseases with a university partner in Abu Dhabi. These are real, but they are a conference and a single specialist deployment, not a portfolio of shipped national infrastructure. The most telling detail is who actually drove Indonesia's flagship AI document. The National AI Roadmap White Paper was led by the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs, Komdigi, which ran the public consultation and coordinated dozens of agencies.
